narrative:
The model estimated a 76% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure to be substantially more likely than success, and that high estimated risk is why your law school application was denied. This is a prediction, not a certainty, but it is the basis for the decision.

The strongest reason was your third-year class rank. You were in the second decile, well below the average of about 5.8 among accepted students, and this factor pushed the prediction most strongly toward bar exam failure. The next most influential factor was your first-year class rank: you were in the third decile, again below the accepted-student average of 6.0, and this also pushed toward failure. Your LSAT score of 38 was the third most important factor. It is slightly above the accepted-student average of about 37.2, so this part of your profile worked in your favor and pushed toward passing, but it was not enough to outweigh the class-rank concerns.

To move forward, ask admissions for specific feedback and whether a later application could be stronger. Consider whether you can improve your academic record or provide context for the early class ranks, and weigh whether retaking the LSAT—despite the solid score—could raise your chances. You may also strengthen your application through relevant legal or professional experience and apply to a balanced range of schools.
